name: HERPES SIMPLEX VIRUS TYPE 1 & TYPE 2 (HSV 1 & 2) QUALITATIVE PCR
interpretation:
Result Interpretation:

•    A "Positive" result indicates Presence of HSV 1 & 2 infection in the individual.

•    A "Negative" result indicates Absence of HSV 1 & 2 infection in the individual.

Clinical Background:

•    Herpes simplex virus (HSV), i.e. HSV-1 & HSV-2 causes various genital & non-genital syndromes. Sites involved include skin, lips, oral cavity, eyes, genital tract, & central nervous system (CNS).Systemic involvement may also occur.

•    PCR detection of HSV DNA in CSF specimens is considered an emerging "gold standard" for the laboratory diagnosis of CNS infections with this virus.

Clinical utility:

•    HSV-1 infections usually involve non-genital areas and HSV-2 infections are primarily found in genital areas, but there is overlap between the two types.

•    Recover of HSV from cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) specimens in culture systems is difficult, and the serologic diagnosis of HSV CNS disease may not be always conclusive, especially during early onset disease. HSV PCR detection from CSF is a sensitive and specific alternative for detection of disease involving the CNS, as well as oral, genital, ocular, and other sites. Vesicle fluid is a preferred specimen rather than discharge from ulcer base.

Limitation of Assay:

PCR is a highly sensitive technique; common reasons for paradoxical results are contamination during specimen collection, selection of inappropriate specimen and inherent PCR inhibitors in the sample. All the results should always be correlated by clinical status and history of the patients. This test is a qualitative assay; results are reported either as negative or positive for herpes simplex virus (HSV) type 1/2.The test does not differentiate between HSV1 and 2.

Reference:

•    Schiffer JT, Corye L: New concepts in understanding genital herpes. Curr Infect Dis Rep Nov 2009;
•    Yi-Wei T, Mitchell PS, Espy MJ, et al: Molecular diagnosis of herpes simplex virus infections in the central nervous system. J Clin Microbiol 1999; 37(7):2127-2136.
•    Mitchell PS, Espy MJ, Smith TF, et al: Laboratory diagnosis of central nervous system infections with herpes simplex virus by PCR performed with cerebrospinal fluid 3. specimens. J Clin Microbiol 1997; 35 (11):2873-2877.
